findings.where: First screen, the hero photograph's backdrop against the slate ground (desktop-01, phone-01). The same grade is described in the palette's 'Slate … the photo's backdrop, keyed', in Texture's 'Graded for the site' sample, and in the motion sketch's hero preview (desktop-02, -03, -06)
findings.fault: Now that the key is off, the photograph's own purple backdrop shows as a large flat rectangle on the slate. Two unrelated dark hues meet with a visible seam: a band of slate runs across the top above the purple, and on desktop the purple fades into slate on the left. The purple is not a house colour, so the hero no longer sits in the house blue-grey. The page also contradicts itself: the palette, the texture sample and the motion preview all show the slate-keyed version, but the hero does not.
findings.who_objects: The founder. The brief for this direction asks for the purple to be graded into the house blue-grey and for every tile to be built in the house colours, and the first screen is what they judge first. A visitor sees a purple box pasted on navy, which looks unfinished rather than refined.

findings.where: Below the 'Articles and talks' list, between the article block and the motion sketch (desktop-06, phone-04)
findings.fault: Two rules are stacked: the list's closing hairline at column width, then the full-width section divider about 65 px below it. Together they read as a double line with an empty strip between them, not one break between sections.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, or the founder judging craft. Every other section break on the page is a single rule, so this one looks like a leftover from moving the talks row out of the article.

findings.where: Footer, the name line on phone ('Mark M. Moseley ·' over the address, phone-05)
findings.fault: When the address wraps to its own line, the middle-dot separator stays behind at the end of the name with nothing after it. It is also set in the small sans beside the large serif name, so it looks like a stray mark.
findings.who_objects: A visitor on a phone, where most of this audience first opens a shared link. The sign-off is the last thing they see, and a dangling dot makes it look unedited.
